title: PostgreSQL Architecture & Process Model
description: Understand the multi-process architecture, Postmaster, shared memory segments, WAL buffers, and background worker daemons.

data.text: Unlike modern threaded database engines like MySQL (InnoDB) or Microsoft SQL Server, PostgreSQL utilizes a **process-based client-server architecture**. Every client connection that connects to PostgreSQL is handled by a dedicated operating system process called a **backend process** (or `postgres` backend worker).

data.caption: PostgreSQL Process and Memory Architecture
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    Client[Client Applications] -->|TCP Connection| Postmaster[postmaster / supervisor]
    Postmaster -->|fork()| Backend[Backend Worker Processes]
    subgraph SharedMemory [Shared Memory Area]
      SharedBuffers[shared_buffers / Data Page Cache]
      WALBuffers[wal_buffers / Transaction Logs]
      CLOG[Commit Log / CLOG]
    end
    Backend <--> SharedMemory
    BackgroundWriter[Background Writer / bgwriter] <--> SharedMemory
    WALWriter[WAL Writer daemon] <--> WALBuffers
    AutoVacuum[Autovacuum Launcher & Workers] <--> SharedMemory
    WALWriter --> DiskWAL[(WAL Segment Files on Disk)]
    BackgroundWriter --> DiskData[(Heap Data Files on Disk)]

rows: Main supervisor process; listens on port 5432 and forks backend processes for new connections.
Dedicated process per client connection that executes SQL queries, plans queries, and returns results.
Flushes modified (dirty) pages from `shared_buffers` to disk progressively to avoid sudden I/O spikes.
Creates periodic checkpoints, flushing all dirty buffers to disk and guaranteeing WAL recovery points.
Flushes WAL buffers to disk sequentially to ensure transaction durability.
Automates dead tuple reclamation and updates planner statistics.

data.title: Process Overhead & Connection Starvation
data.text: Because each client connection allocates an OS process consuming 5MB to 10MB of memory, having 2,000 direct connections can consume 20GB of RAM purely on process overhead! This is why external connection poolers like PgBouncer or Odyssey are mandatory in high-traffic applications.
What Happens When You Send a Query
Understanding the round trip makes every later performance topic — planning, caching, WAL, checkpoints — easier to reason about.

data.caption: Lifecycle of a single SQL statement
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Client sends SQL] --> B[postmaster accepts connection]
    B --> C[Dedicated backend process]
    C --> D[Parser: syntax tree]
    D --> E[Rewrite: views and rules]
    E --> F[Planner / optimiser chooses plan]
    F --> G[Executor reads shared_buffers]
    G --> H{Cache hit?}
    H -->|yes| I[Return tuples]
    H -->|no| J[Read heap page from disk]
    J --> I
    I --> K[WAL written before commit]
    K --> L[Rows sent to client]

data.text: Every process and memory structure the diagram shows is visible through system views. This is the fastest way to answer "how many connections are actually active right now?" in an incident.

data.title: Reading Backends, Memory, and WAL From SQL
data.content: Run these on any running instance.

data.text: Shared Memory: Where the Real Work Happens

`shared_buffers` is PostgreSQL's own page cache (8 KB pages by default). It sits **in front of** the operating system page cache, so a read may be satisfied from shared memory, then from the OS cache, and only then from disk. A common starting point is 25% of RAM on a dedicated server, and on the largest machines 8–16 GB is often plenty.

`work_mem` is different: it is allocated **per sort or hash operation**, not per connection. A single query with three joins can allocate `work_mem` several times, so raising it globally is a classic way to cause out-of-memory kills.

data.title: The Classic Pool-Sizing Trap
data.text: Because each connection is an OS process, `max_connections = 500` with a 10 MB footprint is 5 GB of RAM before any query runs. Use PgBouncer in `transaction` pooling mode and keep the real connection count in the low hundreds per instance.
WAL, Checkpoints, and Why Periodically Everything Pauses

Write-ahead logging guarantees durability: a change is written to the WAL and flushed to disk **before** the transaction is reported as committed. The data pages themselves are written lazily by the background writer. A **checkpoint** forces all dirty pages to disk and records a point from which crash recovery can begin; a badly configured checkpoint is the usual cause of periodic latency spikes.

data.title: Force and Observe a Checkpoint
data.content: Useful in a lab to see the I/O effect; never do this in production on a schedule.
data.code:
-- Ask for an immediate checkpoint and time it
CHECKPOINT;

-- Tune the checkpoint so it spreads writes instead of bursting
-- postgresql.conf
-- max_wal_size = 4GB                 # WAL accumulated before a checkpoint is forced
-- checkpoint_timeout = 15min        # upper bound between checkpoints
-- checkpoint_completion_target = 0.9 # spread the write over 90% of the interval
-- checkpoint_flush_after = 256kB    # control OS writeback batching

items.question: Why does PostgreSQL use processes instead of threads?
items.answer: Historical forking model with strong isolation: a crash in one backend cannot corrupt others, and extensions can be written safely in different languages. The cost is higher per-connection memory, which is why connection pooling is standard practice.

items.question: What is the difference between the background writer and the checkpointer?
items.answer: The background writer continuously trickles dirty pages to disk to smooth I/O; the checkpointer guarantees that all dirty pages up to a consistent point are flushed so crash recovery has a known starting point.

items.question: Do readers block writers in PostgreSQL?
items.answer: No. MVCC gives every statement a snapshot, so reads never take shared locks that block writes. Writers can still block each other on the same row.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: The `postmaster` forks one backend process per client connection; each carries real memory cost, so pool your connections.
`shared_buffers` is PostgreSQL's page cache and `work_mem` is per sort/hash operation — tuning them incorrectly causes memory pressure.
WAL is flushed before commit, which is what makes ACID durability real; checkpoints bound how much WAL must be replayed after a crash.
`pg_stat_activity` plus `SHOW` commands let you observe the architecture live during an incident.
data.takeaway: "Process-per-connection + shared_buffers + WAL before commit" is the architecture answer interviewers want.
